This argument leaves out how the ACA actually regulates insurance companies and how the money flows. Under the Affordable Care Act, insurers are legally required to spend at least 80 to 85 percent of premium dollars on patient care and quality improvement. This is the Medical Loss Ratio requirement. If they do not meet it, they must refund the difference to consumers. That rule alone makes it impossible for insurers to simply pocket ACA dollars, and it has already returned billions of dollars to families and small businesses.

The claim that ACA subsidies go straight to big insurance is also wrong. Premium tax credits go to people, not insurers. The subsidy caps how much a household pays based on income, and the tax credit only fills the gap between that cap and the actual market premium after someone enrolls and receives coverage. If no one enrolls, no insurer gets paid. There is no blank check, no bailout, and no direct transfer of cash to insurance companies.

Rising insurance profits are not proof that the ACA was designed to enrich insurers. Health care costs in the United States are high because hospital systems have consolidated, drug prices are extreme, and provider market power drives prices up. The ACA did not create those costs. It limits how much of those costs can be passed on to families and requires insurers to spend the vast majority of premium dollars on actual care rather than administration or profit.

Removing or weakening subsidies will not lower premiums. It will cause premiums for people who buy their own insurance to double or triple starting in January, because families will suddenly be responsible for the full, unsubsidized price of coverage. That does not reduce the cost of health care, it simply shifts it onto households and forces many to drop coverage entirely. And even though the 80 percent spending rule would still apply, higher unsubsidized premiums mean insurers collect more total dollars per enrollee, which can actually increase insurer profits while fewer people remain insured.

The expanded credits that critics call COVID era were extended because premiums were rising and middle class families were being priced out. Keeping them in place has helped drive uninsured rates to historic lows. Attacking those credits does not hurt insurers, it hurts the people who rely on them to afford coverage.
